analysis.one_liner: Lets states pool federal health funding into a single state-run universal coverage plan.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any House floor action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let any state — or a group of states — apply to Washington for a waiver to combine the federal money it now spends on that state's residents through Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA tax credits, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE into one state-administered health plan. Every resident would be covered, and benefits and out-of-pocket protections would have to be at least as good as what federal programs provide. States would need to reach 95 percent coverage within five years or risk losing the arrangement.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of any state whose government chooses to apply: the uninsured would gain coverage, and people currently paying high premiums or facing big deductibles would get a plan at least as comprehensive and affordable as what federal programs offer [S2]. American Indians and Alaska Natives who enroll would pay no premiums or cost-sharing, with the federal government covering those costs [S2][S3]. States that saved money on administration could reinvest it in health services [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: Any state could apply to waive the usual rules of major federal health programs and instead run one comprehensive plan covering all its residents, with benefits and affordability protections at least as strong as the federal programs being replaced [S2][S3].

The state would receive the federal money that would otherwise have been spent on its residents through Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA premium tax credits, FEHB, and TRICARE, adjusted for caseload growth and medical inflation, plus any administrative savings it achieves [S3].

States must cover 95 percent of residents within five years, with a grace period and technical assistance before a waiver could be terminated, and an independent five-year review of coverage, affordability, and quality [S2][S3].

American Indians and Alaska Natives enrolled through a state plan would face no premiums, deductibles, or copays, with the federal government bearing those costs, and states could not force them to enroll [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal spending is designed to be budget-neutral: states must submit a ten-year plan costing the federal government no more than it would have spent otherwise [S3]. If a state's plan costs more than the federal passthrough, state taxpayers would bear the gap. Private health insurers in an adopting state would lose most of their market, and employers now paying premiums could see that cost shift into taxes or state contributions in that state.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds no new federal money: states must submit a ten-year plan that is budget-neutral for the federal government, so a state wanting richer coverage or faster universal enrollment has to find state revenue to cover the gap [S3].

States that fail to reach 95 percent coverage face a 12-month grace period and then possible termination of the waiver, which could force residents back onto fragmented coverage mid-implementation [S3].

Coordinating a single state plan across Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, FEHB, and the tax code is a large administrative lift, and the bill requires five federal departments and agencies to agree on a joint process [S3].
A state could later repeal its law and opt out, so the guarantee is only as durable as each state's politics [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in a state that opts in, the upside is large: guaranteed coverage with protections at least as strong as Medicare, Medicaid, or ACA plans, and no federal deficit cost by design. The serious catch is financing: because the federal passthrough only matches existing federal spending, a state that wants to actually insure everyone affordably must raise state money, and wealthier or high-cost states face the hardest math. The 95-percent-or-lose-it rule adds pressure that could destabilize a plan in a bad budget year. On balance a genuinely helpful option for states, with real execution and financing risks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee and four other committees without ever getting a markup or a vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on June 8, 2021, with 24 original cosponsors.
It was referred to five House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Oversight and Reform, and Education and Labor — and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No committee ever held a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the House floor.
It drew 27 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no action after the June 2021 referrals through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and everyone whose revenue depends on the current multi-payer system are better off, because no state gained the option to replace private coverage with a public plan.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all 27 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: In any state that adopted a universal plan, most private insurance markets — marketplace plans, much of employer coverage, and Medicare Advantage — would be replaced by a state public plan, wiping out that revenue. Insurers could still sell coverage for benefits the state plan does not offer and could be hired to administer the plan, but their core gatekeeping role would shrink sharply [S3].
A single state payer would cut uncompensated care and administrative billing costs, but would also replace negotiated private rates with state-set payment rates, so gains and losses vary by provider.
Employers in an adopting state would no longer arrange private coverage for workers under the waived rules, shrinking the broker and third-party administration business built around employer plans.
